_readme: Every module at this repo's root MUST have an entry here, and CI fails if one does not —
including modules that own nothing. An explicit empty `resources` with a `why` is a decision;
a missing entry is an oversight, and the two must not look the same.
`resources` lists the external things this module OWNS: the table it writes, the endpoint it
calls. Consumers register these in their own .shared-resources.json, which is what makes the
inlining gate able to see a re-implementation. check-resource-registration.mjs compares the two
and fails a consumer that imports a module without registering its resources.
Match the OPERATION, not the name. A rule that fires on a legitimate read of a table this module
writes is a rule people learn to skim past.

adPlatforms.why: NOT expressible as a resource match, and the attempt is worth recording. A rule on the platform hostnames was tried and flagged 17 sites across 11 repos, every one legitimate: the cookie-banner component (deliberately per-repo, because brand styling differs — and it is what actually loads the tags), the CSP host lists this module exports constants for, and Playwright assertions naming the hosts they expect to be absent before consent. The real contract here — 'adding a platform is ONE entry in AD_PLATFORMS' — is about where a REGISTRY ENTRY goes, not about who may name a hostname. A gate cannot see that distinction, and a rule firing on 17 correct sites is one people would disable. Enforced by review and by repo CLAUDE.md instead.

admin.why: takes a caller-supplied client and answers an owner-tier question. The privilege rule itself lives once, in the DB (see the auth/admin standard) — this module owns no external resource of its own.

alerting.why: a pure decision function: it is handed the current failures plus the previous state and returns which are new. It reads and writes nothing — the caller chooses where to persist the returned state (a heartbeat row, a JSON file), because that store is the caller's, not this module's. No resource match was added: the thing worth forbidding is hand-rolled alert suppression, and that has no reliable textual signature — any regex broad enough to catch it would fire on every ordinary comparison against a timestamp. Enforced by review and by the estate alert-quality standard instead. Note this module has a deliberate Node/CommonJS twin outside this repo for the scheduled agents, which cannot import TypeScript; the two must change together and this file is the canonical spec.

resources.reason: an audit row written by hand can skip the shared action slugs and the request-context parsing, producing rows that look valid and cannot be correlated. Reading audit_log is fine.
the BartMail HTTP API must never be called — optins are a direct Supabase write through this module. Standing rule, predates the module.

a contact_tags write can SEND EMAIL: the AFTER INSERT trigger feeds tag_enrolment_outbox, matched on tag name + tenant, NOT brand. Hand-writing this is how a bulk tool fires an unrelated brand's sequence.

charts.why: pure number/currency formatting. No external system, nothing to own.

resources.reason: consent must persist in a cookie scoped to the registrable domain. localStorage is keyed by ORIGIN, so a localStorage-backed banner re-prompts on every subdomain — including a checkout mid-payment.

three repos each grew their own writeHeartbeat inside lib/cron.ts; two drifted on updated_at and nothing noticed, because no file was named cronHeartbeat.ts for the filename gate to catch. Matches the WRITE only — the status dashboard and staleness watcher read it legitimately.

the per-run history row is written by the same module as the heartbeat, and for the same reason — an inline copy drifts on the duration/started_at handling and, worse, on the never-throws contract. Matches the WRITE only: a history view and a retention sweep read and delete it legitimately.
send pacing, the 2/sec API cap and retry handling live in this module. A direct call bypasses all three and can trip the rate limit for every other sender.

the shared client carries retry handling a hand-rolled token fetch does not. NOTE: one consumer keeps a deliberate local graph.ts (Drafts support the shared module lacks) — that repo allow-lists it rather than pretending otherwise.

jsonLd.why: pure escaping before embedding structured data in a script tag. No external system.

nextRedirects.why: Owns no external resource — it is a list of Next.js redirect rules, consumed by next.config.ts via a RELATIVE import, because the Next config loader does not resolve tsconfig path aliases. A resource match is also the wrong tool here: the thing worth enforcing is that every site SPREADS SHARED_REDIRECTS, which is an ABSENCE, and the inlining gate can only see presence. That check lives in each consumer instead — if public/ holds any .md, next.config.ts must import SHARED_REDIRECTS. Live verification is separate again, in the security-audit agent, because a config that exists is not proof of a config that works.

postgrestFilters.why: pure string functions over a filter grammar. Owns no external system, so there is nothing to resource-match — the re-implementation risk is covered mechanically instead, by scripts/check-postgrest-filter-terms.mjs, which fails any interpolation of a term into a like/ilike filter that does not route through this module. That gate is the resource match for this one.

resources.reason: the shared module is fail-open and applies the spamtrap rule. A direct call can accept addresses this one blocks, and burns the 4,300/day account-wide credit cap.

a hand-rolled sanitise call drifts from the shared forbid-lists, and silently deletes embedded ld+json schema unless the caller reimplements the extract-validate-reattach carve-out — which two consumers had each written separately, one of them noting in a comment that it mirrored the other. Sanitisers with no jsdom dependency (sanitize-html, remark-html's own sanitize) are a DIFFERENT operation for a different runtime constraint and are deliberately not matched here.

safeHtmlNoDom.why: the jsdom-free twin of safeHtml, for serverless and edge runtimes where the DOMPurify/jsdom chain throws at module load. Deliberately NO resource match on `sanitizeHtml(`: a direct sanitize-html call is not a re-implementation of this module, it is the same primitive this module wraps, and at least one consumer route calls it directly for exactly the runtime reason this module exists — a gate firing on that would flag the correct code. What must not be re-implemented is the extract-validate-reattach ld+json carve-out, which has no reliable textual signature; the safeHtml entry's DOMPurify match already covers the version of that mistake a gate can see.

resources.match: iabjs:|Java object is gone|Object Not Found Matching Id|translate_http
resources.reason: these are the fingerprints of third-party scripts injected into a page the app did not write — an in-app-browser bridge, an extension's DOM walker, a translation proxy. They have no reason to appear in application code for ANY other purpose, so a file naming one is a hand-rolled copy of this module's filter. That copy is what the module exists to stop: at consolidation the estate had three filter families spread over the repos, not one repo carried all three, and the iOS and Android halves of the SAME in-app-browser bug had each been found and filtered in a different repo with neither aware of the other. Deliberately NOT matching `window.webkit.messageHandlers` (a plausible legitimate feature-detect for native bridging) or `NEXT_REDIRECT` (legitimately named in middleware and tests) — a gate that fires on correct code is one people learn to skim past.

security.why: crypto and comparison primitives operating on caller-supplied values. Its security comes from the keys it is given, never from what it talks to.

resources.reason: search logging and article writes share ranking assumptions with the reader; a second writer drifts them apart silently.

resources.why: A site must NOT write a support ticket itself. BartMail owns the pipeline, and the spam gate (denylist, allowlist, AI sender classification, daily cost cap) runs there — a direct insert skips all of it and fills the helpdesk with the rubbish the gate exists to stop. This module POSTs to BartMail's /api/support/form-ticket instead. Matches the WRITE: the helpdesk app reads and updates these rows constantly and legitimately.

Same reason, plus one specific trap the endpoint handles: the body goes in body_text, never body_html. A contact form is public input, and a site writing it as HTML turns its own form into a stored-XSS path into the agent console.

resources.reason: a hand-rolled Telegram post skips the delivery check — the API answers 200 with {ok:false} for some errors and 404 for a revoked token, both of which resolve the promise happily — and skips the 4096-character cap, where an over-long alert is rejected entirely rather than truncated. Both failure modes are silent, on the channel whose whole job is to be heard when the primary one is not.

uploads.why: MIME sniffing, filename safety and size validation on bytes the caller already holds. It talks to nothing; the storage client stays in the consuming app.

validation.why: pure predicates over strings. No external system.
